aiOverview.content: The U.S. Department of the Treasury is taking over management of federal student loans in a multi-phase transition from the Department of Education. Initial efforts focus on transitioning roughly 9 million defaulted accounts to Treasury for collections and repayment support. This move is part of a broader plan to move all federal student loans to the Treasury. Key Details on the Transition Defaulted Loans First: The initial phase, announced in March 2026, involves moving ~$180 billion in student loans that are in default (over 270 days behind) to the Treasury. Future Phases: The Treasury will eventually take over the entire ~$1.7 trillion federal student loan portfolio. Purpose: The move is part of the Trump administration’s initiative to shrink the Education Department and centralize debt collection, utilizing the Treasury's ability to manage, collect, and potentially garnish wages through the IRS for delinquent borrowers. Action for Borrowers: For now, most borrowers should continue making payments through their current federal servicer until instructed otherwise, according to Business Insider. Impact of the Shift Collection Focus: The Treasury will take over, focusing on bringing defaulted borrowers back into good standing. No Immediate Changes for Most: Borrowers in good standing or in active, up-to-date repayment plans likely won't see immediate changes to their daily payments, though this is expected to change in later phases. Defaulted Borrowers: Those in default will see their debt management moved from Federal Student Aid (FSA) to the Treasury. This is a developing story with the transition officially announced to start in March 2026, as reported by NPR and AP News.
